A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same contextual-calibration study and contain readable main text and appendices. Matching models, prompts, experiments and retained results establish continuity despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on Distributions and Probabilities, plus a Matching Pennies comparison with human participants (Tables 1–3).

after.justification: v2 retains original model and human results and adds Wordproblems evaluations, template-robustness experiments and corpus-frequency analyses.

M1.justification: The fixed language models, calibration prompts, aggregation of tokenization probabilities and human-study n-gram opponent are retained. The revisions concern evaluation and diagnostic analysis, without introducing a new model, training objective or calibration procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds 33.6K Wordproblems covering scenarios such as tree species and occupations, and uses Dolma number-frequency data for original corpus analysis. These broaden the represented contexts and data sources. Probabilities is renamed Colors, while Distributions and the human study remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated LM panel and principal heuristic baselines remain. However, v2 Tables 4 and 11 report Pick First/Second for Distributions, where v1's corresponding tables reported random baselines. Several Random-temperature and Pick Higher-weight comparisons from v1's aggregate baseline sweeps are omitted.

E3.justification: Relative entropy changes from an entropy ratio to an entropy difference. v2 also introduces compatibility-rate summaries, a WD < 0.05 success criterion and experiments with 500 introductions and 500 additional templates. The stated numeric scales change from numbers under 10/100/1000 to 1–10/10–100/100–999; this establishes revised protocol reporting, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds template-robustness tests, analyses of when models achieve good calibration, correlations between models' color hierarchies, and number-frequency analyses (Appendices D–H). Conversely, v1's detailed per-digit distribution heatmaps and numerical unprompted-versus-prompted human-study comparison are no longer fully reported.

E5.justification: v1's main model tables report point estimates, although its human study already includes randomness tests. v2 adds option-pair-clustered uncertainty estimates, 95% confidence intervals, paired Chat–Base intervals and correlation significance reporting. These substantially change statistical reporting; they do not establish additional seeds or repeated runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds Wordproblems results, template-test outcomes, successful-calibration counts and frequency/hierarchy correlations. Retained benchmark estimates also change: GPT-4o's Probabilities/Colors WD is 0.42 in v1 Table 2 and 0.40 in v2 Table 4. Given revised setting descriptions, this is an updated result rather than an established same-setting gain. Prompted human-study scores remain, but unprompted columns are removed.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 changes RE from H(Π)/H(P) to H(Π)−H(P), moving the calibrated reference from one to zero. v2 also defines the frequency-gap quantity used in its new analysis. These are limited mathematical-definition changes; neither version supplies a substantial theorem or proof development.

C1.justification: The central claims of poor calibration, mode collapse and option-order bias remain. However, v2 elevates training-data number-frequency effects from speculation in v1's discussion to an explicit contribution and an abstract/conclusion finding, substantially extending the paper's explanatory claims.

C2.justification: v1 reports little shared structure between color hierarchies and no obvious explanation; v2 identifies correlated hierarchies and suggests a training-data explanation. It also interprets differing frequency associations across Base and Chat models, acknowledges occasional successful calibration, and adds specific limitations concerning corpus proxies, synthetic templates and restricted numeric coverage.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the SciPy Wasserstein implementation, number-frequency query details, approximately 48 hours on eight A100 GPUs, and an MIT license. It points to a different data/experiment release folder. Both versions still describe release prospectively, so actual availability is not established by the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around linguistic and pragmatic calibration, mathematical capabilities and training-frequency effects. New references include Mielke et al., Tsvilodub et al., McCoy et al., and the Dolma/infini-gram work. Several earlier general training and GAN references disappear; publication updates to retained works are not new citations.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. Results are reorganized from dataset-based sections into metric-based sections, followed by dedicated bias analyses. The human study moves to Appendix I, and the appendices are rebuilt into explanatory sections followed by corresponding figure sections.

P2.justification: The main text switches to two columns, combined result tables are split by metric, and numerous statistical and frequency displays are added. Per-model heatmaps are consolidated into overview grids with revised legends and separate compatibility/distance views. Detailed digit-distribution plots are removed.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence that the findings extend beyond v1's narrow color templates through Wordproblems and the additional-template tests, while clustered confidence intervals improve assessment of model differences. Frequency analyses also turn earlier speculation into measured associations. These gains outweigh remaining reporting problems, including Tables 2 and 10 retaining an ideal RE of one despite the new zero-reference definition; the frequency evidence also remains correlational.
